text:
**Short answer:** For most household fridges, a station with about **1,000–1,500 Wh** of capacity covers most of a day, and about **2,000 Wh** covers a full 24 hours. Whatever you buy, it needs a surge rating of at least about **1,200–1,300 W** to start the compressor, plus a **pure sine wave** inverter.

**Three things to check**

1. **Running watts:** A typical full-size fridge runs at about 100–250 W while the compressor is on. Almost any 1,000 W-class station handles this ([3], [4]).
2. **Surge watts:** The compressor's startup spike is roughly 1,200–2,400 W for a household fridge. A station whose surge rating is too low will trip at the first startup, no matter how much battery it has ([3], [5]). This is the spec most likely to block a fridge.
3. **Watt-hours:** A fridge cycles on and off, so it runs only about 30–40% of the time. A 150 W fridge averages roughly 50–70 Wh per hour after losses ([3], [4]). One guide estimates about 1,000 Wh for most of a day and 1,600–2,000 Wh for 24 hours ([3]). Another estimates about 1,400 Wh per day for a typical 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge, and 2,800 Wh for two days ([5]).

**Choosing a size**

- **Under 12 hours or a few hours:** Around 500–1,000 Wh, provided the surge rating is at least 1,200 W.
- **About one day:** Around 1,400–2,000 Wh.
- **Two days or more:** Around 2,800 Wh or more, or an expandable system.

For a more exact number, check your fridge's yellow EnergyGuide label (kWh per year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 gives average watts) or look up the model in the DOE Refrigerator and Freezer Energy Rating Search Tool ([2], [5]). Bigger, older, or side-by-side fridges use more energy.

**Models mentioned in the results**

I couldn't find direct manufacturer product pages in these results, so these links go to the guides where the models appear. Search the brand's site for the product itself.

- **BLUETTI AC180:** 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W AC, 2,700 W peak, listed at $399–699 ([3](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
- **BLUETTI AC180P:** 1,440 Wh, 1,800 W AC, 2,700 W surge, $649 when checked on Oct 15, but sold out at that time ([5](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2:** 1,070 Wh, about $499 ([4](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- **Anker SOLIX C1000:** 1,056 Wh, about $470 ([4](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- **Anker SOLIX S2000:** 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W AC, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave. The vendor's blog recommends it for fridge backup, so treat that as marketing ([7](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)).

The Bluetti AC200L (2,048 Wh) appears on a deal page ([1](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l)). That page earns a commission on purchases, and I couldn't verify its discount code, so check the price at the store yourself.

Most of these sources are supported by affiliate links, so verify the specs and prices on the manufacturer's site before you buy. If the outage is long or you need to run other appliances, add their wattage to the fridge's before you size the unit.
